questions.question: Define homozygous and heterozygous conditions with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define homozygous and heterozygous conditions with examples. [K]/[CO1]
  • Homozygous condition- An individual is homozygous for a specific gene when they inherit two
  • identical alleles for that trait from both parents. Types- 1. Homozygous dominant: Has two dominant
  • alleles. Eg. TT for tall plants; 2. Homozygous recessive: contains two recessive alleles.
  • Eg. tt for dwarf plants.
  • Heterozygous condition- An individual is heterozygous for a specific gene when they inherit two
  • different alleles for that trait-one dominant and other recessive and the dominant trait is expressed.
  • Eg. Tt (Tall plants). (Homozygous and Heterozygous conditions- 1.5 marks each)

questions.question: Explain why a freemartin is usually sterile. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain why a freemartin is usually sterile. [U]/[CO2]
  • When twin calves of opposite sex are born, one is normal male and the other is usually a sterile
  • female with male like traits and is called ‘Free martin’. During early development, the fusion of
  • blood vessels allows the blood of one embryo to enter the blood stream of other. Male hormone
  • influence the development of female embryo into male direction. Because male sexual
  • differentiation occurs earlier than female differentiation, male hormones- primarily Anti-Mullerian
  • Hormone (AMH) and testosterone produced by the developing testes of the male twin cross into
  • the female twin's bloodstream and suppress her reproductive development. This exposure leads to
  • the degeneration of her Mullerian ducts and arrests ovarian development, leaving her with
  • rudimentary or absent internal reproductive organs, non-functional ovaries and XX/XY leukocyte
  • chimerism, ultimately rendering her permanently sterile. (Brief account- Liberal valuation)

questions.question: Identify and explain the significance of a darkly stained chromatin body in the nucleus of a female somatic cell. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Identify and explain the significance of a darkly stained chromatin body in the nucleus of a
  • female somatic cell. [A]/[CO2]
  • The darkly stained chromatin body found in the nucleus of a female somatic cell is known as a Barr
  • body (or sex chromatin). which represents a heavily condensed and transcriptionally inactive X
  • chromosome. Its biological significance lies in dosage compensation, a mechanism that equalizes X-
  • linked gene expression between males (XY) and females (XX) by randomly silencing one of the two
  • X chromosomes during early embryonic development. This process ensures that females do not
  • produce double the amount of X-linked gene products compared to males, maintaining proper
  • cellular homeostasis. (Identification- 1 mark, significance- 2 marks)

questions.question: Explain why an A→G substitution is classified as a transition, whereas an A→T substitution is classified as a transversion. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain why an A G substitution is classified as a transition, whereas an A T substitution is
  • classified as a transversion. [U]/[CO3]
  • An A to G substitution is classified as a transition because it involves the replacement of one purine
  • (adenine, possessing a double-ring structure) with another purine (guanine), thereby preserving the
  • same chemical ring-structure category. In contrast, an A to T substitution is classified as a
  • transversion because it involves the replacement of a purine (adenine) with a pyrimidine (thymine, a
  • single-ring structure), shifting between two entirely different chemical categories of nitrogenous
  • bases. (Transition- 1.5 marks, Transversion- 1.5 marks)

questions.question: Describe how a mutation occurring in a somatic cell can become restricted to a particular tissue or cell lineage. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe how a mutation occurring in a somatic cell can become restricted to a particular
  • tissue or cell lineage. [U]/[CO3]
  • When a mutation occurs in a somatic cell post-zygotically, it is passed down exclusively to all mitotic
  • progeny derived from that original cell through subsequent cell divisions. As embryonic development
  • or adult tissue renewal progresses, progenitor and stem cells undergo clonal expansion to populate
  • specific organs and structures. Consequently, if the mutation happens within a progenitor cell
  • destined for a particular lineage, all descendant cells within that specific tissue will inherit the
  • mutation, while the rest of the body's tissues remain unaffected because somatic mutations are
  • confined locally and are not transmitted to other independent cell lineages or to offspring.
  • (Liberal valuation)

questions.question: Define mutagens and list their major types with one suitable example each. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define mutagens and list their major types with one suitable example each. [K]/[CO3]
  • Environmental or external agents that induce mutations are called mutagens. It is divided into two
  • major groups: 1. Physical Mutagens-(a) Ionising radiations- radiations with short wavelengths and
  • strong energy like X-rays, protons, neutrons, alpha, beta and gamma rays from radioactive sources.
  • (b) Non-ionizing radiations: UV rays results in pyrimidine hydrates and pyrimidine dimers (Thymine
  • dimers). 2. Chemical Mutagens- (a) Chemicals mutagenic to replicating and non replicating DNA-
  • Eg. Alkylating agents such as nitrogen and sulphur mustards, methyl and ethyl methanesulfonates-
  • add ethyl and methyl groups to bases and alter the base pairing potentials (7-ethyl guanine base pairs
  • with thymine), Hydroxylating agents, nitrous acid (deamination of adenine to hypoxanthine and
  • cytosine to uracil). (b) Chemical mutagenic only to replicating DNA. Eg. Acridine dyes and Base
  • analogs (5-bromo uracil: thymine analog and 2-amino purine : adenine analog).
  • (Definition- 1 mark, Physical and chemical mutagens with example-1 mark each)

questions.question: List the major levels of chromosome organization. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• List the major levels of chromosome organization. [K]/[CO4]
  • Each chromosome consists of a single, enormously long linear DNA molecule associated with
  • histone proteins that fold and pack the fine DNA thread into a compact structure called chromatin.
  • Nucleosomes is the basic structural and functional unit of chromatin. Nucleosome core consists of a
  • complex of eight histone proteins-two molecules each of histone H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 and double
  • stranded DNA that is 146 nucleotides long. The formation of nucleosomes converts a DNA molecule
  • into a chromatin thread about one-third of its initial length and provides first level of DNA
  • packaging. H1 pulls nucleosomes together into a 30-nm fiber (40 fold, second level). 30 nm fiber
  • folds into a series of radial loops and organizes chromatin into distinct functional sections within the
  • interphase (third level). Chromatin is folded more than 100 fold during mitosis or meiosis, the looped
  • domains undergo additional coiling and compression assisted by condensing and cohesion proteins
  • (fourth level). (3/4 marks for each levels- full marks)

questions.question: Describe Morgan's experiments in Drosophila involving grey-bodied, long- winged and black-bodied, vestigial-winged flies, with a neat labelled illustration, and explain his findings. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Morgan’s experiments in Drosophila involving grey-bodied, long-winged and
  • black-bodied, vestigial-winged flies, with a neat labelled illustration, and explain his findings.
  • [U]/[CO2]
  • Morgan's findings revealed that the genes for body color and wing size are physically located on
  • the same chromosome and exhibit genetic linkage, meaning they tend to be inherited together as
  • parental combinations rather than assorting independently as predicted by Mendelian principles.
  • However, the appearance of a small percentage of recombinant offspring (17%) demonstrated
  • that linkage is incomplete, as homologous chromosomes undergo crossing over during meiosis to
  • exchange genetic material and produce novel allele combinations. Furthermore, Morgan and his
  • colleagues established that the frequency of these recombinants correlates directly with the
  • physical distance between the genes. He showed that coupling and repulsion are two phases of
  • linkage corresponding to linkage and crossing over. (Explanation- 3 marks, Diagram- 2 marks)
  • No. Character Dominant Recessive

questions.question: Describe chromosomal sex determination in humans, indicating the sex- chromosome constitution and gamete types of males and females. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe chromosomal sex determination in humans, indicating the sex-chromosome
  • constitution and gamete types of males and females. [U]/[CO2]
  • In man, the chromosomal mechanism of sex determination is of XX-XY type. The total
  • compliment of human chromosomes includes 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes. Female is
  • homogametic, XX, since all gametes are same and produces only one type of egg (22+X) while
  • male is heterogametic, producing two different gametes, (22+X) and (22+Y). The sex of the
  • offspring is determined during fertilisation by the kind of sperm that fuses with the egg. The X
  • bearing sperm produces females (XX) and the Y bearing ones produces males (XY). The testis
  • determining factor (TDF) gene in Y chromosome exhibit a dominant effect for the expression of
  • maleness. A single Y chromosome is sufficient to produce testis and male characteristics.
  • (Chromosomal Sex type in man- 3 marks, Male-1 mark, Female- 1 mark)

questions.question: List the major numerical chromosomal aberrations and state their basic characteristics. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• List the major numerical chromosomal aberrations and state their basic characteristics.
  • [K]/[CO3]
  • Numerical aberrations: Aneuploidy: Condition in which one or few extra chromosomes are
  • added or one or few chromosomes are missing from the basic chromosome sets. Usually arise
  • through non-disjunction of chromosomes in meiosis. Two types: Hypoploidy- Aneuploidy
  • involving loss of chromosomes. Eg. Monosomy-(2n-1), Nullisomy (2n-2). Hyperploidy- Involves
  • addition of chromosomes. Eg. trisomy (2n+1)-Down syndrome (trisomy 21)- autosomal trisomy.
  • Aneuploidy of autosomes and sex chromosomes have been reported in man. Examples for
  • Aneuploidy and autosomal abnormalities. Down syndrome- most common autosomal
  • abnormalities in man, due to autosomal trisomy of chromosome number 21, the affected
  • individuals have 47 chromosomes (2n+1) which is due to non-disjunction that occurs in the
  • meiotic division of either parent. Edward syndrome- trisomy 18. Patau syndrome- Trisomy13.
  • Euploidy, which involves alterations in the number of complete sets of chromosomes. Within
  • euploidy, variations include monoploidy (possessing a single set of chromosomes, n), usually
  • occur in higher plants and polyploidy (possessing three or more complete sets, such as triploidy
  • or tetraploidy), both of which alter entire genomic sets. Polyploids can be autopolyploids- when
  • same genome is duplicated or allopolyploids- multiplication of chromosome sets that are initially
  • derived from two different species. (Types- 2.5 marks, Characteristics-2.5 marks)

questions.question: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the structure of a lampbrush chromosome. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the structure of a lamp brush chromosome.
  • [U]/[CO4]
  • Lampbrush chromosomes are exceptionally large meiotic chromosomes found predominantly
  • during the diplotene stage of prophase I in vertebrate oocytes, characterized structurally by a
  • central backbone of tightly condensed sister chromatids punctuated by darkly staining granules
  • called chromomeres. Extending perpendicularly and symmetrically from these chromomeres are
  • pairs of lateral chromatin loops that are actively undergoing transcription, giving the chromosome
  • a brush-like appearance. There are two types of loops- Complex and plain loops. These
  • chromosomes are highly active in RNA synthesis. The loops consist of transcriptionally active
  • DNA which can synthesize large amount of mRNA.
  • (Description- 3 marks, diagram- 2 marks)

questions.question: Briefly explain the genetic and physiological basis of cystic fibrosis. / [CO5] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Briefly explain the genetic and physiological basis of cystic fibrosis. [U]/[CO5]
  • Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder. It is characterized by
  • accumulation of mucus in the lungs, pancreas and liver, resulting in chronic infections and
  • malfunction of these vital organs. CF gene was mapped to long arm of chromosome 7. Cystic
  • Fibrosis Transmembrane conductance Regulator (CFTR) is a CF gene product and forms ion
  • channels through the membrane of cells that line respiratory tract, pancreas, sweat glands,
  • intestine and other organs and regulates the flow of water and salts across the membrane.
  • Although CFTR forms chlorine channels, it also regulates the activity of several other transport
  • system such as potassium and sodium channels. Since mutant CFTR does not function properly
  • in CF patients, salt accumulates in epithelial cells and mucus builds upon surfaces of these cells.
  • The presence of mucus on the lining of respiratory tract leads to chronic, progressive infections
  • by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and related bacteria. These infections
  • results in respiratory failure and death. CF genes are also pleiotropic and therefore
  • malfunctioning of pancreas, liver, bones and intestinal tract are common in individuals with CF.
  • CFTR also plays a role in regulating lipid metabolism and transport. 70% of cases of CF are due
  • to ΔF 508 trinucleotide deletion. (Genetic basis- 2.5 marks, Physiological manifestations- 2.5
  • marks).
